summary:
Ghost Rovers is an interactive web experience that tells the stories of 13 pieces of NASA hardware left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Users choose a world, then choose a machine, and each one tells its own story in the first person. Every machine has a 3D model that can be turned 360 degrees and enlarged. Each world has its own music and sound effects, and the background shows stars, galaxies and a solar system. The stories come in three reading levels (child, teen and adult), so the same history works for different ages.
It addresses the challenge by turning real mission facts, such as launch and landing dates, sites and how each mission ended, into a narrative instead of a list. The details are based on NASA mission pages and archives.
It matters because young space fans mostly hear about active missions. Ghost Rovers shows that retired machines paved the way for today's achievements and tomorrow's exploration.
details:
Ghost Rovers is an interactive website about 13 NASA machines left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. You tap a planet, choose a machine, and read its story in the machine's own voice. You can also turn its 3D model 360 degrees and tap it to enlarge it. The stories use real mission facts, such as launch and landing dates, landing sites and how each mission ended.

What benefits does it have?

  • It turns facts that are usually in dense technical pages into short stories.
  • It runs in any browser on a phone, tablet or computer, with no install.
  • Child, teen and adult reading levels let one project work for different ages.

What is the intended impact?
We want young space fans to feel a personal connection to the explorers that came first, and to see that retired machines made today's missions possible.

What tools and languages did we use?

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  • The Canvas 2D drawing API for the animated space background (stars, galaxies, a solar system and shooting stars)
  • Three.js for the 3D models
  • The Web Audio API for all the music and sound effects, which are generated in the browser
  • Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, to help write the code, stories and presentation
  • NASA mission pages and the NSSDCA catalog as the sources for the facts

How is it creative?

  • Each machine tells its own story in the first person.
  • Each world has its own music theme.
  • The 3D models are drawn in two styles, glowing line art and solid.
  • Shooting stars burst out whenever you pick a machine.
  • The project is original and uses no copyrighted images or audio.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accuracy: The challenge stresses it, so we based the facts on NASA sources and kept each story short.
  • Audience: Three reading levels cover different ages.
  • Accessibility: It works on phones and tablets and has a sound on/off button.
  • Simplicity: It's easy to explore and doesn't need an account.
  • Honesty about AI: The project credits Claude on the last slide and in the game.
